findings.title: Backup code validation has a read-then-write race condition allowing double use
findings.body: In the credentials authorize() handler, a backup code is validated by decrypting `user.backupCodes`, finding the matching index (`backupCodes.indexOf(...)`), and only afterwards persisting the invalidated code back to the DB (`backupCodes[index] = null` followed by `prisma.user.update`). There is no transaction, row lock, or atomic conditional update between the read and the write. Two concurrent login attempts (or an attacker replaying a captured request) using the same backup code can both read the un-invalidated code, both pass validation, and both succeed in logging in before either write completes — violating the single-use guarantee that backup codes are supposed to provide. This should use an atomic update (e.g. a conditional update keyed on the still-encrypted blob, or a per-code DB row with a unique/used flag) instead of decrypt → compute in memory → re-encrypt → write.

findings.title: Backup code comparison is case sensitive but codes are generated lowercase
findings.body: Backup codes are generated in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts via `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")`, which always produces lowercase hex characters (0-9a-f). However, when matching the user-supplied code here (`credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")`) and in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts (`req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")`), no case normalization (e.g. `.toLowerCase()`) is applied before the `indexOf` comparison. Mobile keyboards/autocapitalize, copy-paste from a capitalized rendering, or a user simply typing uppercase hex letters will cause a valid backup code to be rejected as `IncorrectBackupCode`, producing confusing lockouts for legitimate users.

findings.title: Backup codes are stored with reversible encryption instead of a one-way hash
findings.body: Backup codes only ever need an equality check to be verified (unlike the TOTP secret, which must be decrypted repeatedly to compute codes). Storing them with `symmetricEncrypt` means that anyone who obtains both the database and `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` can recover all ten plaintext backup codes for every user, rather than being limited to verifying a guess as with a proper one-way hash (e.g. bcrypt/sha256 with per-code comparison). Using a one-way hash would reduce the blast radius of a database/key compromise for this specific secret.

findings.title: Misleading "missing_backup_codes" message tells users to regenerate codes in settings, but no such feature exists
findings.body: The new string `"missing_backup_codes": "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings."` is shown when a user's `backupCodes` column is null but 2FA is otherwise enabled. However, there is no settings UI or API endpoint added in this PR (or elsewhere) that lets a user regenerate backup codes without fully disabling and re-enabling two-factor authentication (which also resets the TOTP secret). The message gives users incorrect instructions and no actionable path to resolve the error.

findings.title: No automated test covers logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code
findings.body: The PR's own TODO (`// TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup`) acknowledges that the actual backup-code authentication paths are untested. The added test only exercises the backup-codes *display* step (download button, copy button, close button) during setup; it never submits a backup code through the login form (apps/web/pages/auth/login.tsx) nor through the "Lost access" flow in DisableTwoFactorModal. Since this is the core new functionality (bypassing 2FA with a backup code) and touches authentication/security-sensitive code, shipping without end-to-end coverage of the actual login/disable-with-backup-code flow is a significant gap.

findings.title: New BackupCode component exported under the wrong function name (copy-paste leftover)
findings.body: `apps/web/components/auth/BackupCode.tsx` is clearly adapted from `TwoFactor.tsx`, but the component function itself is still declared as `export default function TwoFactor({ center = true })` instead of `BackupCode`. This is cosmetic for the default export, but it means React DevTools, error stack traces, and any code that inspects `Component.name` or `displayName` will show "TwoFactor" for two completely different components, making debugging and future refactors confusing.

findings.title: Backup-codes download Blob URL is never revoked when the modal is cancelled, leaking memory
findings.body: `handleSetup` creates a Blob URL via `URL.createObjectURL(textBlob)` and stores it in `backupCodesUrl`. The only place the previous URL is revoked is right before creating a new one inside `handleSetup` (`if (backupCodesUrl) URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl)`). `resetState()` (used when the user cancels the modal or closes it after setup) resets `password`, `errorMessage`, and `step`, but does not revoke `backupCodesUrl` nor reset it to an empty string. If a user completes/cancels the 2FA setup flow without triggering another `handleSetup` call, the created Blob URL is never released for the lifetime of the page, leaking memory.

findings.title: Backup code request field is used without type/presence validation before calling string methods
findings.body: `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` assumes `req.body.backupCode` is always a string whenever it is truthy, but request bodies from an API endpoint are not type-checked. If a client (or an attacker probing the endpoint) sends a non-string value for `backupCode` (e.g. an object or number), `.replaceAll` will throw a runtime TypeError that is not caught anywhere in the handler, resulting in an unhandled exception/500 instead of a clean 400 validation error.
